title: Detection of Search Open Websites/Domains
summary: This detection strategy covers adversary collection from open websites and domains, including company pages, social media, job adverts and public code repositories. An attacker uses that material to learn your technology stack, your staff and your future plans before sending a message or probing an address. The telemetry that helps is reverse proxy access logs, bot management or web application firewall records, search referral data where it is available, and canary documents placed on public pages. It fails in practice because the activity looks like ordinary browsing or legitimate search engine crawling, and the requests often come from shared cloud address space that you cannot attribute to a person.

beginner.definition: Open source information means anything that is public and free to read. It includes your company website, job adverts and social media pages. An attacker reads these pages to learn how your company works. This detection watches for somebody reading many public pages in a short time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your public pages are meant to be read, so you cannot simply block them. But the way a visitor reads them tells a story. A normal visitor opens a few pages and leaves. A collector opens every team page, every job advert and every technology post in a few minutes. That pattern shows preparation for an attack. Catching it early gives your team time to harden exposed services and to warn staff about coming phishing.
howItWorks: Every request to your public site is written to a reverse proxy or web server access log.
The detection groups those requests by source address and by browser user agent string.
It counts how many different paths the same source reads inside a short window.
It also measures how many sensitive public pages that source reached before it stopped.
A source that reads far more pages than a normal visitor is flagged for analyst review.
beginner.example: Think of a shop with a large window display. Anyone may stop and look, and that is good for business. But one person stands outside for an hour and photographs every item, the alarm box and the staff door. The shopkeeper cannot accuse that person of a crime, because the window is public. He can, however, note the time, the description and how often the person returns. Your detection is the shopkeeper notebook. It records unusual reading habits on public pages so that a human can decide what they mean.
takeaways: Public pages cannot be hidden, so you detect the reading pattern instead.
Many different pages from one source in a short time is the key signal.
Crawler traffic must be filtered, or your alert queue will overflow.

objectives: Define open source collection and name the public pages attackers value.
Describe how a web access log records a collection attempt.
Write a query that counts distinct request paths per source address.
Separate legitimate crawlers from abusive collection activity.
Explain how early warning supports hardening and staff awareness.
dataSources: Reverse proxy access logs with source address, request path, status code and user agent string
Web application firewall or bot management logs with request rate per source address
Canary document or tracking pixel alerts triggered when a public file is opened
Content delivery network request logs for static pages, job adverts and datasheets
Search engine referral logs showing which queries led visitors to your public pages
logic: The pattern is a single source reading an unusually wide set of public pages in a short time, especially pages that describe teams, technology or hiring. The fields that must be correlated are the source address, the user agent string, the request paths and the timing between requests, plus any canary that fires when a seeded document is opened. Benign traffic comes from search engine crawlers, marketing research tools and candidates reading job pages, and those sources usually declare themselves in the user agent or stay inside one section of the site. The malicious case reads across unrelated sections, ignores robots directives and often uses a plain generic user agent.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Wide Enumeration of Public Site Sections by One Source
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     status_code: 200
#     url_path|contains:
#       - '/careers'
#       - '/about'
#       - '/leadership'
#       - '/technology'
#   filter_crawlers:
#     user_agent|contains:
#       - 'bot'
#       - 'crawler'
#       - 'spider'
#   condition: selection and not filter_crawlers | count(distinct url_path) by src_ip > 60
# level: low
falsePositives: Search engine crawlers that index the whole site without declaring a bot user agent.
Recruitment agencies and job boards that read many career pages in one session.
Accessibility or website quality testing tools run by your own marketing team.
A journalist or industry analyst researching the company for a legitimate article.
tuningNotes: Baseline normal daily request volumes per page group before you set the threshold, because a large site naturally produces big counts. Filter declared crawler user agents from major search engines, then keep an unfiltered low severity branch for everything else. Scope the rule to pages that carry technology, staff or hiring content. If you raise the threshold too far you lose the patient collector who reads a few pages each day, so also alert on new sources that appear in your logs every day for a week.
